Cheat sheet

INST1 Memorization Sheet

Print this and keep it in your tool bag. The Installer 1 written exam rewards recall of the cabling system's parts and distances, the rules for spaces, pathways, bonding, and firestop, the limits on every pull, the color codes, and what a tester is telling you. Every name and number on this sheet is fair game.

01The exam itself

FactValue
CredentialBICSI Installer 1 (INST1): the entry-level installation certificate for the ICT trades. It is nonrenewable
Two partsA hands-on exam first, then the written exam. Both must be passed. The written exam can only be taken after the hands-on is passed
Hands-onSix tasks done to industry standards, 20 minutes per task. The proctor gives pass or fail after each task
Hands-on timingGiven on the last day of the IN101 class, generally Friday afternoon
Hands-on retestOne failed task may be retested the same day at no cost. Failing the same task twice, or failing two tasks, means retaking the hands-on on another date
Written exam75 multiple-choice questions testing knowledge and application, 2 hours, computer-based at a Pearson testing site
Tools at the written examA calculator and a whiteboard are provided. There are no scheduled breaks
Passing scoreSet by a panel of experts using a standard-setting method. BICSI does not publish it. A failing candidate gets a score report by topic area, not a score
Experience requiredNone. Recommended: the IN101 class, about 50 hours of self-study, and safety and PPE training
Physical requirementsTell colors apart, work with good manual dexterity, stand for long periods, climb ladders, and lift and carry up to 50 pounds
ApplicationAt least seven days before the hands-on date
Exam fee$335 for a BICSI member, $400 for a nonmember. It covers the first hands-on attempt and the first written attempt
Retest fee$135 member, $200 nonmember
Virtual walk-in hands-on$135
Waiting periods30 days between unsuccessful attempts; 90 days after a third unsuccessful attempt
Eligibility windowOne year from your first hands-on attempt
IdentificationA government photo ID with your signature plus a secondary ID. The name must match your BICSI profile
Next stepsInstaller 2 Copper (INSTC) and Installer 2 Optical Fiber (INSTF). The design path later leads to the RCDD
How the questions readJobsite scenarios that ask for the FIRST step, the MOST likely cause, or the BEST method or material
Area of expertiseWeight on the examQuestions in this course's 50-question tests
1. Field Planning, Implementation, and Design13%6
2. Pathways and Spaces31%16
3. Pulling Copper and Fiber Cable21%11
4. Terminating Copper and Fiber Cable15%8
5. Testing6%3
6. Troubleshooting6%3
7. Retrofits3%1
8. Integration and Convergence3%1
9. Codes and Standards2%1
Pathways and Spaces (31 percent) and Pulling (21 percent) together are more than half the exam. This course's official-format test uses 75 percent. BICSI does not publish its passing score, so treat 75 percent as a target, not a prediction.

02The cabling system

Part of the systemWhat it is and what it holds
Work area (WA)Where people use the system: the outlet, the patch cord, and the equipment on the desk. Two outlets minimum per work area
Horizontal cabling (HC)The cable from the outlet in the work area back to the patch panel in the telecom room on the same floor
Telecommunications room (TR)Serves one floor or part of one. Holds patch panels, racks, switches, and the cross-connects for horizontal and backbone cabling
Telecommunications enclosure (TE)A cabinet that serves a small space on a floor. It is never a substitute for a TR
Backbone cablingThe cable between TRs, equipment rooms, and entrance facilities. Cabling between two TRs is backbone, even on one floor
Equipment room (ER)Serves the whole building or campus. Houses large common equipment and terminates backbone cabling. It can also serve as an entrance facility
Entrance facility (EF)Where outside cabling enters the building. Holds the protectors, the demarcation, and the primary bonding busbar
Structured cabling system (SCS)The whole planned system of subsystems above, built to one standard. A building's information transport system (ITS) is the same idea
Main cross-connect (MC)The top of the backbone hierarchy, usually in the equipment room
Intermediate cross-connect (IC)The optional middle level between the main cross-connect and a floor's horizontal cross-connect
Horizontal cross-connectWhere horizontal cabling meets the patch panel and equipment, normally in the TR
Telecommunications outletThe wall or furniture jack that ends the horizontal cable, in the work area
Topology ruleValue
ShapeA hierarchical star: every floor reaches back to a higher level, never in a ring or a chain
Cross-connects in the horizontalOne level only. No tandem patch panels between the outlet and the TR
Cross-connects in the backboneAt most two levels: the main and one intermediate
Bridged taps and splicesNot allowed in horizontal copper cabling
DistanceMetricEnglish
Horizontal permanent link90 m295 ft
Horizontal channel (the link plus the cords)100 m328 ft
Patch and equipment cords, all together10 m33 ft
Multimode optical fiber backbone, structured cabling maximum2000 m6562 ft
Singlemode optical fiber backbone, structured cabling maximum3000 m9842 ft

Work area planning

  • At least two outlets per work area: one for voice, one for data, at minimum
  • A work area is planned at about 10 square meters (108 square feet) of floor space
  • The outlet and the station equipment count as the work area; the patch cord ends it
  • Application distances can be much shorter than the maximums above; the application sets the real limit
  • The 90 m permanent link leaves room for the cords: 90 + 10 = 100 m channel
  • Horizontal cabling ends in a TR on the same floor as the work area it serves
Think of the permanent link as what the installer builds and the channel as what the user runs. Cords add the last 10 m. Never use cable longer than 90 m in the permanent link to make a distance work.

Twisted-pair cableRated frequencyNotes
Category 5e100 MHzMinimum category for new installation, 4 pairs, 24 AWG typical
Category 6250 MHzOften has a spline or a tighter twist to control crosstalk
Category 6A500 MHzThe A is augmented; larger overall diameter, so it fills pathways faster
Cable constructionWhat it means

F/UTPFoil over the whole cable, no shield on the individual pairs
STPShielded twisted pair: a general name for cable with a shield around the pairs or the whole cable
S/FTPBraid over the cable and foil on each pair; the shield must be bonded
23 AWG and 24 AWGConductor sizes; the lower the number, the thicker the wire. Category 6A is often 23 AWG
Solid conductorUsed for permanent horizontal runs and punched down on an insulation displacement connector
Stranded conductorUsed for patch cords; it flexes without breaking but loses more signal, so cords stay short
MultipairBundled pairs for backbone voice cable, in 25-pair binder groups
Color-coded binderA colored ribbon or thread that groups every 25 pairs inside a large multipair cable
Optical fiber typeCore sizeJacket color you will see
OM1 multimode62.5 micronOrange

OM3 multimode, laser optimized50 micronAqua

Fiber constructionValue or rule
Cladding diameter125 micron for both multimode and singlemode
Tight bufferA 900 micron coating on each fiber. Used inside buildings, easier to terminate, less water-resistant
Loose tubeCoated fibers with a 250 micron coating floating in a gel or dry tube. Used outdoors, must be transitioned inside the building
Multimode light sourceLED or VCSEL, at 850 nm and 1300 nm
Singlemode light sourceLaser, at 1310 nm and 1550 nm
Jacket color is voluntaryThe color is a convention, not a law. Read the print on the jacket for the real fiber type
StrandColorStrandColor

Fiber color code: Blue, Orange, Green, Brown, Slate, White, Red, Black, Yellow, Violet, Rose, Aqua. Strands 13 to 24 repeat the same colors with a black tracer, except the black strand, which takes a yellow tracer.
Coax cableImpedance and use
RG-675 ohm. The standard for video and cable television runs; the best choice in new work
RG-5975 ohm. Older and thinner, with more loss; short video runs and closed-circuit cameras

04Codes, listings, and standards

TermMeaning
CodeA rule adopted into law, enforced by an inspector. The NEC is a code once your jurisdiction adopts it
StandardA consensus document that sets the technical method. It becomes enforceable when a code, a contract, or a specification calls for it
AHJAuthority having jurisdiction: the inspector, fire marshal, or building official whose decision wins. Mounting heights and permit rules are the AHJ's call
NRTLNationally recognized testing laboratory, such as UL. It lists and labels products
ListedA product that an NRTL has tested and put on a published list for a stated use
Specification versus drawingWhen they disagree, ask the designer in writing before you build. Do not guess
Copper ratingWhere it may be installed
CMPPlenum: air-handling spaces. The highest rating for communications cable
CMRRiser: vertical runs between floors, through a firestopped opening
CMG and CMGeneral purpose: horizontal runs on one floor, but not in plenums or risers
CMXLimited use: dwellings and raceways only, in short runs
Fiber and coax ratingWhere it may be installed
OFNPOptical fiber, nonconductive, plenum
OFNROptical fiber, nonconductive, riser
OFNOptical fiber, nonconductive, general purpose
OFCPOptical fiber, conductive (it has metal in it), plenum
OFCROptical fiber, conductive, riser
CATVPCommunity antenna television and coax, plenum
CATVRCoax, riser
CATVCoax, general purpose
Substitution ruleDetail
A higher rating can replace a lower oneA plenum cable may go where a riser or general cable is required; a riser cable may go where a general cable is required
A lower rating can never replace a higher oneGeneral cable in a plenum or a riser is a violation, even for a short run
Order from highest to lowestPlenum (P), then riser (R), then general (G or none), then limited (X)
Cable type must match its spaceThe jacket print tells you the rating. If the print is missing, treat the cable as unrated
Standards familyWhat it covers
TIA-568The cabling standard: topology, distances, performance, connectors, and test methods
TIA-569Pathways and spaces: rooms, trays, conduit, and boxes
TIA-606Administration: labeling and records
TIA-607Bonding and grounding for telecommunications
TIA-758Outside plant, at recognition level only
ISO/IEC 11801The international structured cabling standard, with its own class names
NFPA 70The National Electrical Code (NEC): wiring, cable listings, bonding, and firestop of penetrations
NFPA 72Fire alarm and signaling, at recognition level. Fire alarm work is separate from structured cabling
OSHAThe federal safety rules for your jobsite: PPE, ladders, trenching, hazard communication
Name the standard, not its edition. The exam asks which document governs a task, not which revision. Local code and the AHJ override a standard whenever they are stricter.

05Telecom spaces and bonding

SpaceWhat it serves and the rules
Telecommunications room (TR)At least one per floor. Placed so that no horizontal run passes 90 m. Horizontal cabling ends in a TR on the same floor
Equipment room (ER)Serves the building or campus. Houses large equipment and terminates backbone and horizontal cabling
Entrance facility (EF)Where public and private service cabling enters the building. Includes the entrance point at the building wall
Telecommunications enclosure (TE)Serves at most 335 square meters (3600 square feet) on a floor. It does not replace a TR
EnvironmentConditioned air, clean and dry, lit well enough to read a label, with power and bonding already in place
Do not put in a TRWater pipes or drains over the equipment, unrelated equipment, storage, and anything that blocks the door
Door and accessLockable, wide enough to move equipment, and clear of obstructions
Work and aisle spaceIf no distance is specified, plan at least 1 m (3.28 ft) around and between equipment
BackboardRule
MaterialPlywood, void free, A grade on the exposed side and C on the wall side, 15 percent moisture or less
Thickness19 mm (3/4 in), recommended; sheets are 1.2 m by 2.4 m (4 ft by 8 ft)
Mounting heightFrom 203 mm (8 in) above the finished floor up to 2.6 m (8.5 ft). Do not split the difference in a taller room
Fire protectionTwo coats of fire-retardant paint. If the code requires fire-retardant treated plywood, do not paint it; ask the AHJ whether to leave the stamp showing
WhereOn at least two walls of a TR; all four if possible. Mount a 305 mm (12 in) tray on the same walls
Fasteners on studsAlign the sheet to the studs. On metal studs, screws at least 12.7 mm (0.5 in) longer than the plywood is thick
Fasteners in a hollow wallToggle bolts at least 6.3 mm (0.25 in) in diameter, 51 mm (2 in) from the edges, about every 610 mm (24 in)
JointsNo gaps between adjacent sheets
Rack and cabinetRule
Width483 mm (19 in) is the standard; 584 mm (23 in) racks are used by service providers
Height2.1 m (7 ft) is the normal height
One rack unit1 U is about 45 mm (1.75 in) of vertical space
AnchoringBolt a floor rack to the floor with expansion anchors, flat washers, and lock washers
Overhead supportBrace the top of the rack to the wall, a tray, or a ladder rack. Seismic bracing is whatever the AHJ requires
AccessUse double-sided racks and keep the front and the rear accessible
Equipment screwsM5, M6, 10-32, or 12-24 threads, with star washers for bonding
Wall-mounted rackLag bolts and washers into the plywood; check the wall will carry the full load
Cable managementVertical managers at the sides, horizontal managers by each patch panel, and room for cord slack
D-ringsFine for small bundles and cross-connect jumpers; never a replacement for a ladder rack
Bonding partRule
Primary bonding busbar (PBB)Formerly the telecommunications main grounding busbar (TMGB). One per building, in the entrance facility, bonded straight to the service ground
Secondary bonding busbar (SBB)Formerly the telecommunications grounding busbar (TGB). One or more per TR or ER, as many as needed
Telecommunications bonding backbone (TBB)An insulated, stranded copper conductor from the PBB to each SBB, equalizing the floors
Bonding conductor for telecommunications (BCT)Connects the PBB to the electrical service's grounding electrode system. Keep it as short as possible
Rack bonding conductorFormerly the TEBC. 6 AWG minimum, stranded, insulated copper from the SBB or PBB to each rack and cabinet
Grounding equalizerA 6 AWG minimum insulated copper conductor that evens out potentials between TRs
Jacket colorGreen, or green with a yellow stripe, for every bonding conductor
LugsTwo-hole compression lugs on every busbar and rack connection
Surface preparationScrape paint to bare metal, apply antioxidant compound, then make the connection
Daisy-chainingNever. Each rack gets its own conductor back to the busbar
Busbar mountingOn insulated standoffs with at least 51 mm (2 in) of clearance behind it
Bend rulesMinimum bend radius of 203 mm (8 in); never a bend of less than 90 degrees
Bonding resistanceTwo-point bonding test: 0.1 ohm (100 milliohms) is the recommended maximum
Conduits and traysMetal conduit, tray, and ladder rack are bonded. A grounding bushing carries a 6 AWG copper wire to the busbar
Power cord groundNever the only ground for a rack. The telecommunications ground path is separate and verifiable
Old and new names: PBB = formerly TMGB; SBB = formerly TGB; rack bonding conductor = formerly TEBC. The exam may use either set, so know both. If a document shows an old name, translate it before you act.

Conduit ruleValue
Fill, one cable53 percent of the inside area
Fill, two cables31 percent
Fill, three or more cables40 percent
Bends between pull pointsNo more than two 90-degree bends
Distance between pull pointsNo more than 30 m (100 ft)
Bend radius, copper cable, trade size 2 in (53 mm) and smaller6 x the inside diameter
Bend radius, copper cable, larger than 2 in10 x the inside diameter
Bend radius, conduit carrying optical fiber10 x the inside diameter
Conduit typesEMT is thin-wall steel tubing, ENT is flexible nonmetallic tubing, and PVC is rigid plastic. Each has its own inside diameter, so look it up before you calculate fill
Pull boxAdd one where a run would otherwise exceed two bends or the pull length; it must stay accessible, never behind a finished wall
Conduit endsReam the cut ends and install bushings so the jacket is not cut
Pull stringLeave one in every empty conduit, and replace it whenever you pull
SweepsUse sweep elbows for fiber and large cables
Entering a TRConduit ends come in at the left side of the backboard. The interconnecting conduit is 78 mm (3 trade size) minimum, bushed and firestopped
EMT trade sizeInside diameter
1/2 in0.622 in
3/4 in0.824 in
1 in1.049 in
1-1/4 in1.380 in
1-1/2 in1.610 in
2 in2.067 in
Fill calculationHow to do it
FormulaFill percent = number of cables x cable OD squared / conduit ID squared x 100
Worked exampleTen cables with a 0.25 in OD in 1 in EMT: 10 x 0.0625 / 1.1004 x 100 = 56.8 percent. That is over the 40 percent limit
FixAt 40 percent, 1 in EMT carries 0.4 x 1.1004 / 0.0625 = 7 of those cables. Use a 1-1/4 in conduit or split the run
Use OD and IDOD is the outside diameter of the cable; ID is the inside diameter of the conduit. Square each one
Round downAlways round the number of cables down, never up
Tray and ladder rackRule
Tubular ladder rack depth38 mm (1.5 in); the width runs from 152 mm (6 in) to about 1 m (3.28 ft)
Threaded rod, heavy duty16 mm (5/8 in) rod, properly anchored
Wire mesh tray supportsWithin 0.6 m (2 ft) of each end and each side of a joint, then every 1.52 m (5 ft)
Rod-stock tray depths51 mm (2 in), 100 mm (3.94 in), and 152 mm (6 in), usually in 3 m (10 ft) sections
Cutting a listed trayAsk the AHJ first. A field cut can void the listing
BondingEvery section is bonded, whether it carries power or low-voltage cable
Fill and depthSet by the designer and the code. Use retaining posts so cable never rises above the side rails
Vertical runsSecure each cable to the rung so the weight spreads over several supports
Riser coreA vertical ladder rack in a riser core passes through firestopped openings
Multiple levelsFirestopping between levels may be required
J-hook and noncontinuous supportRule
Maximum spacing1.5 m (5 ft) apart
SagEven and shallow; the cable bundle must not rest on the ceiling or touch the tile grid
AttachmentNever to ceiling grid wires, to the grid itself, or to another trade's conduit, duct, or pipe
Independent supportHang from the structure above with its own rod, strap, or beam clamp
LoadDo not exceed the hook's rated cable count; use bigger hooks or a tray
Fiber cordsKeep them off solid-bottom supports; use mesh, ladder, or noncontinuous supports to avoid pressure points
Separation from power and EMI sources (circuits above 5 kVA unless stated)Minimum distance
Branch circuits of 5 kVA or lessNo extra separation needed
Unshielded power in open or nonmetal pathways610 mm (24 in)
Unshielded power next to a grounded metal pathway305 mm (12 in)
Power in grounded metal conduit next to a metal pathway152 mm (6 in)
Electric motors and transformers1220 mm (48 in)
Fluorescent, neon, mercury vapor, and discharge lamps130 mm (5.12 in)
Arc welders800 mm (31.5 in)
Induction heating equipment1000 mm (39.37 in)
Power wiring creates electromagnetic interference (EMI), and radio sources create radio-frequency interference (RFI). Distance and grounded metal pathways reduce both. When a table and the designer disagree, the stricter distance wins.
Outlets and boxesRule
Single-gang and double-gang boxesA box for one or two faceplates; deep enough for the cable bend radius
Cut-in ring or old-work bracketMounts a faceplate in existing drywall without a box
Low-voltage mounting bracketNever in a fire or smoke barrier unless listed for it
Poke-throughA rated floor assembly installed to its listing; the cables in it must match the space below
Floor boxFed through a floor core or a slab sleeve and firestopped to the listing
Furniture feedA power pole or partition raceway; keep power and communications on separate sides
Mounting heightSet by the drawings and the AHJ; never guess it
Plenum boxesA surface raceway in a plenum needs plenum-rated cable
Sleeve, core, and slotRule
SleeveA short pipe through a wall or floor. Bushed at both ends
CoreA round hole drilled through a floor or wall. Core where the drawings show; never into structure without approval
SlotA rectangular floor opening for a riser. Frame it and firestop it
Spare capacityLeave room for growth; do not fill a sleeve to its limit
FirestopEvery sleeve, core, and slot with cable through it gets a listed firestop system
Unused openingsCap and label them, and firestop them too if the wall is rated

07Firestopping

ConceptRule
Firestop systemA listed system: a tested combination of materials and method for one specific penetration, in one specific wall or floor assembly
WhyTo keep flame, heat, and smoke from passing through the opening and to restore the rating of the wall or floor
F ratingHow many hours the system keeps flames from passing through. It also withstands a hose stream
T ratingHow many hours the system keeps the temperature rise on the cold side below a limit
L ratingHow well the system seals against smoke leakage
Listing numberThe tested system has an identifier such as a letter code and a number. Read it from the approval sheet, then match the system exactly
Smoke barrierA wall built to resist smoke, not just flame. Penetrations in it also need sealing
Mechanical systemsManufactured, presized elastomeric components (modules, blocks, grommets) held in place by mechanical compression, sometimes in a frame. Durable, and they can be reconfigured
Nonmechanical systemsPliable materials molded or sized to the opening: putties, caulks and sealants, blankets, pads, foams, pillows, and intumescent wraps. Intumescent materials expand with heat; passive ones are endothermic or ablative
Putty padsSeal the back of an outlet box in a rated wall
RuleDetail
Restore the ratingWhatever hole you make, you close with a system that restores the wall's rating
Match the listed system exactlyThe wall type, penetrant, opening size, and material must all match the tested system
Label itMark the firestop with the system number, the date, and the installer
Inspect itThe AHJ or inspector must accept it before it is covered
Reseal after any changeAdding or removing a cable breaks the seal, so reseal the opening every time
End of the dayA penetration in a fire or smoke barrier is sealed at the end of every workday, not just at the end of the job
Never useFoam, tape, rags, or insulation as a substitute for a listed system
Not your callIf you cannot find a listed system that fits, stop and ask the designer or the AHJ

08Pulling cable

Setup itemPurpose
Reel stands or boxesLet the cable unwind without twisting or kinking
Sheaves and rollersGuide the cable around corners at its bend radius
Pull string or ropeCarries the pulling force, not the cable jacket
Grips and eyesAttach to the cable with a swivel so the pull does not twist it
CommunicationRadios or signals between the pulling end and the feed end
Pull scheduleLists each cable, its label, its length, and the sequence of the pull
Mark before cuttingLabel the cable before you cut it from the reel
Pulling limitValue
Tension, 4-pair cable110 N (25 lbf) at most, per cable
Bend radius, 4-pair UTP4 x the cable OD
Bend radius, multipair copper10 x the cable OD
Bend radius, optical fiber with no load10 x the cable OD
Bend radius, optical fiber under pulling tension20 x the cable OD
Manufacturer limitsWin over the numbers above whenever they are stated
KinksA kinked cable is damaged. Replace it
CrushDo not crush a cable with ties, staples, or a tight J-hook; leave bundles loose
FillNever exceed the conduit fill limits just to get one more cable in
LubricantOnly a lubricant listed as compatible with the cable jacket
Riser pullMethod
Top downFeed from the top with a reel brake at the feed end and support at each floor to take the weight
Bottom upUse a pull line with a winch, a swivel, and tension monitoring
Cable weightHeavy backbone cable needs hooks, grips, and supports in proportion; secure it at each floor
FirestopEvery floor opening is firestopped once the cable is in place
LabelLabel the cable at every floor; never splice a riser
SlackAmount
Work area, 4-pair copper305 mm (12 in) minimum after termination; not stored in loops
TR or ER, 4-pairEnough to reach the farthest corner by way of the pathway, plus floor to ceiling
TR or ER, multipairThe length of the backboard plus floor to ceiling
TE2 m (6.6 ft) stored outside the enclosure
WhyService slack allows reterminations and moves without a new cable
Fiber handlingRule
Where to pullOn the strength member (the aramid yarn or central member), never on the fibers or the jacket
Figure-eightLay long runs in a figure eight on the floor to avoid twist, and flip it as you feed
InnerductPull fiber inside an innerduct in conduit and trays, and leave the end of the duct labeled
CleanlinessCap the ends, keep dirt out, and never drag cable across a dirty floor
Pulling tensionStay below the maximum on the cable's specification sheet

09Termination

Before you terminate

  • Confirm the cable label matches the pull schedule and the outlet or port label
  • Check the pair twist and the jacket for kinks, nicks, or crush
  • Leave the service slack, then strip only the jacket needed
  • Untwist at most 13 mm (0.5 in) for Category 5e and above
  • Use the right tool for the connecting hardware: punch-down tool, termination tool, or cleaver
  • Keep the jack's wiring standard the same at both ends of the link
  • Choose one wiring standard per job and mark it on the drawings
  • Verify the work area outlet type matches the drawings and the jack color rules
PinT568AT568B
1White-greenWhite-orange
2GreenOrange
3White-orangeWhite-green
4BlueBlue
5White-blueWhite-blue
6OrangeGreen
7White-brownWhite-brown
8BrownBrown
Wiring ruleDetail
One standard per jobPick T568A or T568B and use it for every jack, panel, and cord in the system
Straight-through patch cordSame standard at both ends
Pair 1Pins 4 and 5, blue pair
Pair 2Pins 1 and 2
Pair 3Pins 3 and 6
Pair 4Pins 7 and 8
Split pairWires from two different pairs land together as a pair; every pin connects, so continuity passes, but crosstalk fails
25-pair color codeColors
Tip colors, in orderWhite, red, black, yellow, violet
Ring colors, in orderBlue, orange, green, brown, slate
Pair 1White-blue
Pair 2White-orange
Pair 5White-slate
Pair 6Red-blue
Pair 25Violet-slate
Formula for pair nTip color = group (n - 1) divided by 5, dropping the remainder. Ring color = (n - 1) mod 5
Larger cablesEach group of 25 pairs gets its own color-coded binder
Connecting hardwareNotes
110 blockA punch-down block for horizontal and backbone cross-connects. Terminate with a 110 tool; the jacks sit on the connecting block
66 blockAn older style punch-down block for voice. A 66 block is for voice only, not for high-speed data
Insulation displacement connector (IDC)The jaw that cuts through the insulation as you punch the wire down
Patch panelA rack-mounted panel of jacks; the horizontal cable punches into the back
JackPunch each pair to its color code on the jack; keep the pairs twisted as close to the terminals as you can
Strain reliefTie off or secure the cable so no pull reaches the termination
CoaxNotes
Connector typesF connector for cable television; BNC for security video
Compression connectorThe standard today: clean cut, correct strip, then compress
StripCut the jacket and the center conductor to the length the connector maker shows
TestCheck continuity and look for a shorted center conductor and shield
Fiber connectorsNotes
LCSmall form factor with a latch; the common choice on new work
SCSquare, push-pull connector; common on patch panels
STRound bayonet connector with a twist lock; older style
MPOA multifiber push-on connector that carries many fibers in one ferrule
UPCUltra physical contact: a polished end face, blue connector body
APCAngled physical contact: a polished angled end face, green connector body
Do not mixNever mate an APC to a UPC; the angled and flat faces damage each other and lose signal
Inspect before you connectLook at the end face with a scope; if it is dirty, clean it
CleaningDry clean first with a cassette cleaner or swab; use a solvent only if the dry clean fails
Never lookNever look into a fiber end or a connector with a light source on

10Testing and troubleshooting

Test typeWhat it covers
Permanent linkThe fixed cable and both connectors, without the patch cords. This is what the installer certifies
ChannelThe whole path including both patch cords, the connectors, and the cross-connect. This is what the user's equipment sees
ParameterWhat it measures
WiremapWhether each pin connects to the right pin at the far end
LengthThe electrical length of each pair; it must stay within the permanent link limit
Insertion loss (IL)How much signal is lost along the link; lower is better
NEXTNear-end crosstalk: signal leaking from one pair into another at the end near the tester
PSNEXTPower sum NEXT: the combined crosstalk from the other three pairs on one pair
FEXTFar-end crosstalk: signal leaking from one pair into another at the far end of the link
ACR-FAttenuation-to-crosstalk ratio, far end: how much stronger the signal is than the noise at the far end
Return loss (RL)Signal reflected back by impedance mismatches, often from a poor termination
Propagation delayHow long the signal takes to travel the link
Delay skewThe difference in delay between the fastest and slowest pair
Wiremap faultLikely cause and fix
OpenA wire is not connected or has been cut. Reterminate the pair or find the break
ShortTwo wires touch. Check for a stray strand or a staple through the cable
Reversed pairA pair is wired tip to ring at one end; reterminate that pair
Crossed pairA pair is on the wrong pins at one end; the jack or the panel was punched in the wrong order
Split pairOne wire from each of two pairs was swapped. The pins connect, but the twist is wrong. Reterminate to the color code
Tester stepWhat to do
Set the referenceDo this at the start of each session, with the matching adapters
Choose the limitPick the permanent link or channel limit for the right category
Choose the cable typePick the cable family and the NVP if the tester asks
AutotestConnect and run the full test
Save with the labelUse the cable label as the name, so the record matches the cable
PASSEvery parameter is within the limit
FAILOne parameter is outside the limit. Find the cause, fix it, and retest
Marginal asteriskThe result passes, but is within the tester's accuracy of the limit. Treat it as a pass only if the specification allows; many do not
Tester accuracyLevel III covers Category 6 up to 250 MHz; Level IIIe covers Category 6A up to 500 MHz
CordsTest with the tester's own cords or adapters, and replace them when they wear
Fiber testingWhat to do
Tier 1 testA light source and a power meter measure total loss in the link. Reference the equipment first, then measure
OLTSOptical loss test set: a light source and power meter in one box
OTDROptical time-domain reflectometer: shows where the loss and reflections are along the fiber. Recognition level
Launch cordA reference cord used so the first connector is also tested
Clean firstInspect and clean every connector before testing
Both wavelengthsTest multimode at 850 and 1300 nm and singlemode at 1310 and 1550 nm

11Safety, labeling, retrofits, and other systems

Safety topicRule
Site safety planRead it on day one and follow it; attend the safety briefing
PPESafety glasses, gloves, hard hat, and safety shoes as the site requires; hearing and dust protection when needed
LaddersInspect before use, face the ladder, keep three points of contact, and never overreach
LiftsBe trained before you operate a lift or scaffold; follow the harness rules
Lockout and tagoutNever work on or near energized equipment that has not been locked out and tagged by the person who controls it
Confined spacesDo not enter a manhole or vault until it is tested, ventilated, and permitted, with a standby person outside
Silica dustDrilling and coring concrete creates silica dust. Use water or a vacuum and wear a respirator
AsbestosIf you suspect it, stop work, keep others away, and report it. Never disturb or sweep it
Laser safetyNever look into a fiber end; treat every fiber as live until it is proven dark
LiftingLift with your legs, ask for help, and carry no more than your limit
First aidKnow where the kit is, who is trained, and how to call for help. Report every injury
ElectricalTreat unknown wires as live; only qualified electricians connect to ac panel grounds
LabelRule
IdentifiersEvery space, cable, panel, port, pathway, and bonding conductor gets a unique identifier
Both endsLabel each cable at both ends, and use the same name on both
WhereWithin sight of the end, where it can be read without moving the cable
Machine printedUse a printed, permanent label; never handwriting that smudges
Match the recordsThe label, the drawing, the panel record, and the tester file must all agree
RecordsKeep the administration records, the as-built drawings, and the test results, and hand them over at closeout
Cable tagsLabel both ends of a bonding conductor and the sheath of a backbone cable at the rack or ladder rack

Retrofits

  • Survey the existing space and pathways before you promise anything
  • Protect the occupied space: dust barriers, floor protection, and moving furniture only with permission
  • Lift and replace ceiling tiles carefully; do not break or stain them
  • Remove abandoned cable under the NEC unless it is tagged for future use
  • Test existing cable before you reuse it; it must meet the category you need
  • Plan the cutover: install, test, and label first, then move users with an agreed outage window
  • Keep the old system working until the new one is accepted
  • Firestop every penetration you make or open

Other systems on the cabling

  • Paging and sound masking
  • Clocks and nurse call
  • Building automation (BAS)
  • Life safety and fire alarm: a separate system with separate rules
  • Elevators
  • Access control
  • Video surveillance
  • Wireless access points (AP)
  • Distributed antenna systems (DAS)
  • Convergence puts many systems on the same cabling; plan the pathways for all of them
Power over EthernetPower at the source
PoE type 115.4 W
PoE type 230 W
PoE type 360 W
PoE type 490 W
Bundle heatingMore power means more heat in a bundle. Use larger-gauge or higher-category cable and smaller bundles for high-power runs
Equipment namesThe switch or injector is the power sourcing equipment (PSE); the camera, phone, or access point is the powered device (PD)
Plan every job around three questions. What does the drawing say, what does the AHJ require, and what does the manufacturer allow? When any of them is stricter than your habit, the stricter one wins.

12Acronyms

Every acronym used in this course, 97 in all.

AcronymStands forMeaning
ACR-FAttenuation to Crosstalk Ratio, Far EndHow much stronger the signal is than the far-end crosstalk noise.
AHJAuthority Having JurisdictionThe inspector, fire marshal, or building official whose decision on a code question is final.
APAccess PointThe wireless radio unit that connects devices to the cabled network, usually through PoE.
APCAngled Physical ContactA fiber connector with an angled end face; the body is green.
AWGAmerican Wire GaugeThe conductor size scale: the lower the number, the thicker the wire.
BASBuilding Automation SystemThe controls that run heating, cooling, lighting, and other building services.
BCTBonding Conductor for TelecommunicationsThe conductor that joins the PBB to the building's grounding electrode.
BICSIBuilding Industry Consulting Service InternationalThe association that runs the Installer 1, Installer 2, Technician, and RCDD credentials.
BNCBayonet Neill-ConcelmanA twist-lock coax connector used on security video and test equipment.
CATVCommunity Antenna TelevisionThe general-purpose listing for coax and cable television cable.
CATVPCommunity Antenna Television, PlenumThe plenum listing for coax cable.
CATVRCommunity Antenna Television, RiserThe riser listing for coax cable.
CMCommunications, generalThe general-purpose communications cable listing: no plenum or riser use.
CMGCommunications, general purposeThe general-purpose communications cable listing, equal to CM.
CMPCommunications, plenumThe plenum communications cable listing: the highest rating, allowed in air-handling spaces.
CMRCommunications, riserThe riser communications cable listing: for vertical runs through a firestopped opening.
CMXCommunications, limited useThe limited-use communications cable listing: dwellings and raceways, short runs.
DASDistributed Antenna SystemA set of antennas that spreads cellular or public safety radio coverage through a building.
EFEntrance FacilityWhere outside cabling enters the building, with the protectors and the primary bonding busbar.
EMIElectromagnetic InterferenceElectrical noise from power wiring, motors, and lamps that can corrupt cable signals.
EMTElectrical Metallic TubingThin-wall steel conduit; a common pathway for horizontal cable.
ENTElectrical Nonmetallic TubingFlexible corrugated plastic conduit, used in some walls and slabs.
EREquipment RoomThe room for equipment that serves the whole building or campus.
FEXTFar-End CrosstalkSignal that leaks from one pair into another at the far end of the link.
FTPFoiled Twisted PairTwisted-pair cable with a foil shield; the F in F/UTP and S/FTP stands for foil.
HCHorizontal Cross-connectThe point on a floor where horizontal cabling is connected to patch panels and equipment.
HDTDRHigh-Definition Time-Domain ReflectometryA tester display that shows where along a link a reflection (return loss problem) occurs.
HDTDXHigh-Definition Time-Domain CrosstalkA tester display that shows where along a link crosstalk is coming from.
HVACHeating, Ventilating, and Air ConditioningThe building systems that move and condition air, including the ducts and plenums above the ceiling.
ICIntermediate Cross-connectThe optional middle level of the backbone, between the main and horizontal cross-connects.
ICTInformation and Communications TechnologyThe trades that install and maintain cabling and the systems that ride on it.
IDInside DiameterThe measure across the inside of a conduit; fill is calculated from it.
IDCInsulation Displacement ConnectorA jaw that cuts through wire insulation as the conductor is punched down.
IECInternational Electrotechnical CommissionThe international body for electrical and electronic standards, a partner of ISO.
ILInsertion LossThe signal lost along the link; lower is better.
IN101Installation 101The BICSI class that prepares a candidate for the Installer 1 hands-on and written exams.
INST1Installer 1BICSI's entry-level installation certificate: a six-task hands-on exam, then a 75-question written exam.
INSTCInstaller 2 CopperThe next BICSI installation certificate after Installer 1, focused on copper cabling.
INSTFInstaller 2 Optical FiberThe next BICSI installation certificate after Installer 1, focused on optical fiber cabling.
ISOInternational Organization for StandardizationThe international body that, with the IEC, publishes the ISO/IEC 11801 cabling standard.
ITSInformation Transport SystemThe cabling and pathways that carry signals through a building or campus.
LCLucent ConnectorA small form factor fiber connector with a latch, common on new work.
LEDLight-Emitting DiodeThe common light source for multimode fiber links.
MCMain Cross-connectThe top of the backbone hierarchy, usually in the equipment room.
MHzMegahertzThe unit for the frequency a cable category is rated to carry.
MPOMulti-fiber Push OnA connector that carries many fibers in one ferrule, used for high-density links.
NECNational Electrical CodeThe model electrical code, published by NFPA as NFPA 70 and adopted into law by each jurisdiction.
NEXTNear-End CrosstalkSignal that leaks from one pair into another at the near end of the link.
NFPANational Fire Protection AssociationThe group that writes the NEC (NFPA 70) and the fire alarm code (NFPA 72).
NRTLNationally Recognized Testing LaboratoryA lab approved to test products and list them for a stated use.
NVPNominal Velocity of PropagationThe speed of signal in the cable as a percent of the speed of light, used to compute length.
ODOutside DiameterThe measure across the outside of a cable; bend radius and conduit fill are calculated from it.
OFCPOptical Fiber, Conductive, PlenumA plenum listing for fiber that has metal strength members or armor.
OFCROptical Fiber, Conductive, RiserA riser listing for fiber that has metal strength members or armor.
OFNOptical Fiber, NonconductiveA general-purpose listing for fiber with no metal parts.
OFNPOptical Fiber, Nonconductive, PlenumA plenum listing for fiber with no metal parts.
OFNROptical Fiber, Nonconductive, RiserA riser listing for fiber with no metal parts.
OLTSOptical Loss Test SetA light source and power meter used to measure total fiber link loss.
OM1Optical Multimode 1A 62.5 micron multimode fiber grade, with an orange jacket.
OM2Optical Multimode 2A 50 micron multimode fiber grade, with an orange jacket.
OM3Optical Multimode 3A laser-optimized 50 micron multimode grade, with an aqua jacket.
OM4Optical Multimode 4A higher-bandwidth laser-optimized 50 micron multimode grade, with an aqua jacket.
OM5Optical Multimode 5A wideband 50 micron multimode grade, with a lime green jacket.
OS1Optical Singlemode 1A singlemode fiber grade for indoor use, with a yellow jacket.
OS2Optical Singlemode 2A singlemode fiber grade for outdoor and long-distance use, with a yellow jacket.
OSHAOccupational Safety and Health AdministrationThe federal agency whose rules govern jobsite safety, PPE, ladders, and hazard communication.
OTDROptical Time-Domain ReflectometerA tester that shows where loss and reflections occur along a fiber.
PBBPrimary Bonding BusbarThe main busbar for telecommunications bonding, one per building, formerly called the TMGB.
PDPowered DeviceThe camera, phone, or access point that receives PoE power.
PoEPower over EthernetPower delivered over the same twisted pairs that carry data.
PPEPersonal Protective EquipmentSafety glasses, gloves, hard hat, shoes, and other gear that protects the worker.
PSEPower Sourcing EquipmentThe switch or injector that supplies PoE power.
PSNEXTPower Sum Near-End CrosstalkThe combined crosstalk that the other three pairs put on one pair.
PVCPolyvinyl ChlorideRigid plastic conduit, commonly used underground or in slabs.
RCDDRegistered Communications Distribution DesignerA BICSI design credential, several steps above the installer certificates.
RFIRadio-Frequency InterferenceNoise from radio transmitters and similar sources that couples into cabling.
RGRadio GuideThe prefix for a family of coax types such as RG-6, RG-59, and RG-11.
RLReturn LossSignal reflected back by impedance mismatches, often from a poor termination.
SBBSecondary Bonding BusbarA busbar in a telecommunications room or equipment room, formerly called the TGB.
SCSubscriber ConnectorA square push-pull fiber connector, common on patch panels.
SCSStructured Cabling SystemA planned, standards-based set of cabling subsystems that serves many applications.
STStraight TipA round bayonet fiber connector with a twist lock, from an older generation.
STPShielded Twisted PairA general name for twisted-pair cable with a shield around the pairs, the cable, or both.
T568ATIA-568 wiring scheme AOne of two standard 8-pin color orders: pin 1 is white-green.
T568BTIA-568 wiring scheme BOne of two standard 8-pin color orders: pin 1 is white-orange.
TBBTelecommunications Bonding BackboneThe insulated copper conductor that ties the PBB to the SBBs between floors.
TETelecommunications EnclosureA cabinet that serves a small area on a floor, never a replacement for a telecommunications room.
TEBCTelecommunications Equipment Bonding ConductorThe older name for the rack bonding conductor, 6 AWG minimum, green, from busbar to rack.
TGBTelecommunications Grounding BusbarThe older name for the secondary bonding busbar (SBB).
TIATelecommunications Industry AssociationThe standards body that writes the TIA-568, 569, 606, and 607 documents.
TMGBTelecommunications Main Grounding BusbarThe older name for the primary bonding busbar (PBB).
TRTelecommunications RoomThe room on each floor where horizontal cabling ends on patch panels.
ULUnderwriters LaboratoriesA nationally recognized testing laboratory that lists cable, firestop systems, and hardware.
UPCUltra Physical ContactA fiber connector with a polished flat end face; the body is blue.
UTPUnshielded Twisted PairTwisted-pair copper cable with no shield; the most common horizontal cable.
VCSELVertical-Cavity Surface-Emitting LaserA low-cost laser used with laser-optimized multimode fiber.
WAWork AreaThe space where people use the system: the outlet, the patch cord, and the station equipment.
